title: Medication infusion pump safety

sources.use: ISMP high-alert medication list (2024): reproduction needs permission

objectives: Verify pump programming at the moments the FDA singles out.
Use the drug library and respond to alerts rather than silencing them.
Obtain an independent double check when policy requires.

items.text: Verify programming (dosage, rate, volume) at change of shift, when any change is made to the settings, when a new bag is hung and when new tubing is primed (FDA).
Label pump channels and tubing at the port of entry with the drug or fluid name if the pump does not display it (FDA).
Use the drug library where one exists and respond carefully to alerts rather than silencing them (FDA).

Obtain an independent double check of pump settings by a second clinician when facility policy requires it for high-risk drugs; the FDA defines this as two clinicians checking separately, alone and apart, then comparing against the order.
Which drugs need a double check and who may programme pumps are set by local policy; ISMP's list identifies high-alert drug classes.

Before use, inspect the pump for signs of breakage or damage (such as small chips or cracks); remove, tag and sequester a damaged pump rather than use it. For high-acuity patients, the FDA calls for having a backup plan to obtain a working pump and tubing quickly.

For high-risk infusions, watch for signs of over- or under-infusion using other available monitoring (for example cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO2 or glucose readings) alongside the pump itself, and monitor the patient and the infusion per facility protocol; a secondary volume check (such as a time strip or buretrol) can help confirm the expected volume has infused.
Pump model, drug-library configuration and manufacturer instructions are unit-specific.
Programming steps follow the manufacturer's instructions and unit training; doses and rates are never taken from this library.

For unresolved pump alerts, programming differences from the medication order or suspected over-/under-infusion, assess the patient immediately, check the pump and ordered therapy, and urgently notify the responsible clinical team. Whether to pause, continue or transfer an infusion depends on the patient's condition, suspected malfunction and facility emergency procedure—not an automatic stop rule.

If a pump fails during a high-risk infusion, remain with and closely monitor the patient while another team member obtains a functioning replacement, following the unit's backup plan. For a patient at risk of fluid overload, the FDA gives clamping/disconnecting tubing as an example of a possible response to prevent over-infusion; that decision is context-specific and must follow local instructions. Report suspected pump problems through the facility's required pathway.
Record programming checks and double checks per unit standard.

checklist.text: Check the order against the drug, concentration and pump programming.
Verify programming at shift change, after any change, with a new bag and with new tubing.
Use the drug library and respond to alerts rather than silencing them.
Obtain an independent double check when policy requires it.
Label the channel and tubing at the port of entry if the pump does not show the drug name.

For an unexplained pump alarm or programming discrepancy, immediately assess the patient, check the order and the pump, and urgently escalate using the unit's pump-failure protocol. Do not ignore possible over-infusion or reflexively interrupt an essential infusion; safely stop, continue or transfer delivery as the patient's condition and the local emergency plan require.

gaps: Drug-specific high-alert strategies, concentration standardisation and smart-pump configuration: not covered.

Pump failure contingency plans for continuously infused high-alert/life-sustaining medicines must be device- and drug-specific; this checklist does not prescribe automatic interruption, temporary delivery methods or replacement-pump programming.
